rv.q: This is a big, bold, entertaining swing at major issues, led with considerable star power.
It is excitingly staged theatre with an ambition as bold as Yvonne’s, seeking to say so much about women, race and the media that still feels incredibly timely.
But for all its fast-paced frenzy-making, the second act of Dyer’s adaptation is messy, with too many scenes that might be either imagined or real, too many conversations that only serve to confuse.
But it’s a shame that the play doesn’t quite live up to its promise thanks, ironically, to its own narrative choices.
The second half, though, is a headlong dive into melodrama that is just too much.
Still, its neatly crafted ambiguity ultimately feels frustrating.
Though Wilson’s play never quite resolves its meaty themes, it remains a stinging indictment of the US’ media culture.
But, amid the zig-zagging story telling, the drama itself goes missing.
Sadly, it doesn't add much to the conversation.
However, all these promising strands fail to cohere, adding little new to the conversation and leading to a rushed, open-ended conclusion.
THE STORY has undoubted merit when it ceases in its attempts to be shocking and instead focuses on the real impact of the media's forensic depiction of stereotypes.

Both the play The Story and reporter Yvonne’s big story suffer from the same issue: a great idea smothered by an overworked device that increasingly becomes a distraction instead of the instrument of the author.
Dyer’s direction is superbly confident, and beautifully realised as characters speak and argue in parallel scenes.

While there are some intriguing and insightful remarks about the injustices faced by black people in American journalism as well as in wider society, the play takes too long to make the point, already known to the savvy and discerning, that mainstream media is not to be trusted.
This is a promising premise, but the play, despite updates to the script for this revival, falls strangely flat.

There are all sorts of interesting and thoughtful possibilities in Tracey Scott Wilson's play The Story, but very few of them are developed or explored in ways that give us a clear story, explore political issues or take some character on a believable journey.
The Story is a highly entertaining piece of drama about the conflict between systems with historically ingrained power structures and outsiders who try to excel within their rigid bounds.
It’s an urgent, tense narrative that feels bang up–to-date.
Toussaint is remarkable in her grand intensity, and Wright manages to just about convince us of what Yvonne is hiding.
However, without that deeper understanding of the characters and their connections, it feels a little underwhelming.
There is a lot of potential to be found in The Story, and it is far from a bad show.
But we wouldn't recommend The Story when today's UK headlines and the reasons behind them would be a more relevant place for this venue to seek to represent the population it's paid to serve.
The Story tries to be bigger than… well… the story, but a single thread tying everything together is missing.
The Story is intense and brilliant with amazing acting, a clever and pacey script and a mystery that keeps you questioning what you think you know.
Fresh, funny and gripping, The Story is storytelling at full throttle.
Wright deftly leads the company through steep character archs and theatrical sweeps from scene to scene, humor to outrage.
Gripping, fast-paced and full of energy, you're certainly unlikely to be bored.
The Story is pacey, unpredictable and moving. Towards the end of the play, it spirals slightly out of control; however, the cast's absolute commitment maintains a level of watchability.

cn.t: Critics find this newsroom thriller timely and provocative on race and media ethics, with Letitia Wright earning praise, but many fault the play's uneven structure, overwrought second half, and failure to fully develop its compelling ideas.
